headline: An Ancient Etymology Finds Bewilderment Inscribed in the Name Allāh
lede: Fred Björn (@Jawnmard1), a writer on Sufism and Islamic mysticism, opens a thread with a classical etymological claim: that the word *Allāh* may derive not from *al-ilāh* (the standard philological account) but from the Arabic root *aliha*, linked to *walah* — a word denoting the overwhelmed, disoriented state of a soul consumed by love. On this reading, God's supreme name means 'that by which intellects become ecstatically crazed.' The argument is not a Sufi invention but a documented position in medieval Arabic lexicography — one that mystics have since inhabited as a map of the spiritual path itself.
body:
The mainstream account of *Allāh*'s etymology holds that it is a contraction of *al-ilāh* — literally 'the deity' — produced by eliding the initial consonant of *ilāh* and fusing it with the definite article. This derivation is supported by pre-Islamic inscriptions, Semitic cognates (Hebrew *ʾElōah*, Aramaic *ʾElāh*), and early Arabic poetry in which *al-ilāh* and *Allāh* appear interchangeable. Classical Basran grammarians also argued the name was *murtajal* — spontaneously coined without any derivable root, an irreducible proper noun for God. Neither account exhausts the classical debate.

The alternative etymology Björn cites is associated above all with **Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī** (d. 1210) in his encyclopedic *al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr*. Rāzī catalogues multiple derivations of *ilāh* in his commentary on the Fātiḥa, among them the claim that it traces to *aliha* in the sense of *tahayyara* — 'to be dumbfounded, stupefied' — such that God is called *Ilāh* because 'the hearts are stupefied because of His immensity.' He adds a closely related variant: that *ilāh* is a phonetically modified form of *wilāh*, from the root *w-l-h*, giving the noun *walah* — an overwhelming love-bewilderment that extinguishes the lover's self-awareness. Rāzī presents these alongside more sober lexicographical options as competing positions within the discipline of *ishtiqāq* (Arabic etymological analysis), not as definitive conclusions.

Sufi thinkers did not invent this etymology, but they gave it a second life by treating it not as philological curiosity but as theological description. **Ibn ʿArabī** (d. 1240) — whose *al-Futūḥāt al-Makkiyya* devotes thousands of pages to the divine names — identified *Allāh* as *al-ism al-jāmiʿ*: the all-comprehensive name that subsumes every divine attribute. For him, the defining encounter with God was *ḥayra* — a technical term for the perplexity that descends when mutually contradictory truths about the divine present themselves simultaneously. Unlike ordinary confusion, *ḥayra* before God is epistemically correct: the intellect is not failing but reaching the outer limit of what intellect can do. **Al-Ghazālī** (d. 1111), in *al-Maqṣad al-Asnā*, opened his treatment of the divine names by observing that 'minds are bewildered by it and the sight of intellects falls far short of its principles' — framing the inquiry in precisely the language that Rāzī's *aliha/tahayyur* etymology implies.

The Sufi vocabulary distinguishes these overlapping states with care. *Wajd* — literally 'finding' — is the acute, temporary state of spiritual ecstasy: an overwhelming sensation that descends on the heart and briefly annihilates self-awareness. *Walah* is more extreme and more durable, a love-bewilderment so total that the lover no longer even perceives the Beloved, having been absorbed into the Beloved. Classical Sufi sources describe its stages as running from lamenting prayer through drunkenness to *talaf* — a total annihilation that paradoxically precedes eternal life in God. The claim that *Allāh* encodes *walah* at its root is, in Sufi terms, a claim that God's name already contains — already *is* — the experiential destination of the entire mystical path.

concepts.definition: An Arabic word (root w-l-h) for overwhelming love-bewilderment, in which the lover is so consumed by the Beloved that they lose their bearings entirely. It encompasses both ecstatic joy and anguished longing and is used in classical Sufi taxonomies to describe an advanced spiritual state surpassing ordinary ecstasy. A person in this state is called wālih — someone whose rational faculties have been displaced by love.

A technical term in Ibn ʿArabī's mystical philosophy for the perplexity that arises when mutually contradictory aspects of divine reality present themselves simultaneously as true. Unlike ordinary confusion, ḥayra before God is considered the highest authentic cognitive response available to humans — the intellect reaching its outer limit rather than failing. Ibn ʿArabī reverses the word's usual negative connotation, making bewilderment a mark of genuine divine knowledge.

An Arabic Sufi term meaning 'ecstasy' or 'finding,' describing the acute, temporary spiritual state in which a sudden overwhelming sensation descends on the heart and annihilates self-awareness. Classical Sufi manuals distinguish it from tawājud (deliberately seeking the state) and wujūd (pure being/finding — the highest stage). It is the event; walah is the condition.

Arabic for 'the all-comprehensive name,' used in Sufi theology to describe Allāh as the supreme divine name that subsumes all other divine attributes. It is often used synonymously with ism al-aʿẓam. The argument is that unlike names for individual attributes (al-Raḥmān, al-Qādir), Allāh alone refers to the totality of the divine Essence.

The 'Greatest Name' of God in Islamic tradition — the supreme divine name believed to encompass all divine attributes and to carry unparalleled spiritual power. Sufi tradition generally identifies it with Allāh itself, though medieval scholars debated whether it referred to a different name or combination of names.

The classical Arabic discipline of etymological derivation — tracing words to their roots and analyzing how meaning flows from root to derivative. Medieval scholars applied ishtiqāq to the divine name Allāh to debate whether it was derived (and if so, from which root) or spontaneously coined without etymological analysis.

An Arabic word for stupefaction or utter bewilderment — the state of being so overwhelmed that rational faculties seize up. In the etymology Rāzī records, aliha is glossed as a synonym of tahayyara ('to be stupefied'), connecting the root of ilāh/Allāh to this cognitive incapacity before the divine.

A term in classical Arabic linguistics meaning 'spontaneously coined' — describing a word that arose as a proper noun without derivation from any prior root. Some Basran grammarians argued that Allāh was murtajal: an irreducible divine proper name that cannot be etymologically analyzed, predating rather than deriving from ilāh.

The 'Beautiful Names of God' in Islam — the ninety-nine divine names or attributes enumerated in the Quran and hadith, such as al-Raḥmān (the Compassionate) and al-ʿAlīm (the All-Knowing). Sufi theology treats Allāh as the master-name that contains and transcends all ninety-nine.

An Arabic verb (root ʾ-l-h) that classical lexicographers glossed as 'to seek refuge with' or, in one tradition cited by Rāzī, as a synonym of tahayyara ('to be stupefied/bewildered'). It is the verbal form invoked in the alternative etymology of ilāh/Allāh, connecting God's name to the stupefaction of the heart before divine immensity.

In Sufi taxonomy of the stages of walah, the final stage — a total self-annihilation in which the lover's individual identity is dissolved entirely into the Beloved. Sufi sources describe it paradoxically as a destruction that precedes eternal life, the limit-point of the mystical path.

Also known as Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb ('Keys to the Unseen'), the encyclopedic Quranic commentary of Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī (d. 1210). One of the most cited works in the Islamic intellectual tradition, it integrates theology, philosophy, jurisprudence, and linguistics in the exegesis of individual Quranic verses, and is the primary classical source for the aliha/walah/tahayyur derivations of Allāh.

The 'Meccan Revelations' of Ibn ʿArabī (d. 1240) — a vast encyclopedic work of Sufi metaphysics spanning hundreds of chapters on cosmology, spiritual stations, and the divine names. It is the foundational text of speculative Sufism and the primary source for the doctrine of ḥayra as the highest mode of divine knowledge available to humans.

books.title: al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr (Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb)
books.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī (d. 1210)
books.summary: An encyclopedic Quranic commentary covering theology, philosophy, jurisprudence, and Arabic linguistics in extraordinary depth. Its treatment of the Fātiḥa is the primary classical source for the multiple etymologies of Allāh/ilāh, including the aliha/walah/tahayyur derivations. An English translation of Volume I by Sohaib Saeed is available and makes this material accessible to non-Arabic readers for the first time.

books.title: al-Futūḥāt al-Makkiyya (The Meccan Revelations)
books.author: Muḥyī al-Dīn ibn ʿArabī (d. 1240)
books.summary: The magnum opus of Ibn ʿArabī, running to thousands of pages on Sufi metaphysics, cosmology, and the divine names — with a single chapter on the Asmāʾ al-Ḥusnā spanning roughly a thousand pages. It is the foundational text of speculative Sufism and the primary source for the doctrine of ḥayra as the defining epistemological encounter with God. William C. Chittick's two-volume SUNY Press study translates and analyzes over six hundred passages.

books.title: al-Maqṣad al-Asnā fī Sharḥ Asmāʾ Allāh al-Ḥusnā
books.author: Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī (d. 1111)
books.summary: Al-Ghazālī's systematic commentary on the ninety-nine Beautiful Names of God, arguing that Allāh is the supreme name because it indicates the Essence in totality rather than any single attribute, and uniquely cannot be applied — even metaphorically — to any other than God. The book opens with the observation that minds are bewildered before the divine names, connecting immediately to the walah/ḥayra tradition. Translated into English by David Burrell and Nazih Daher for the Islamic Texts Society.

Based on the opening post, the thread likely continues through additional classical derivations or Sufi commentaries on the Divine Name, consistent with the account's sustained focus on Islamic mysticism, Persian literature, and the inner dimensions of Sufi practice.
